lead: Posture for height is the belief that fixing anterior pelvic tilt or rib flare adds centimetres. Forum users report gains of one to two inches after stretching and strengthening.
Clinical literature on pelvic tilt concerns spinal alignment, pain and disability; no study located measured height change.

paras: Believers say a tilted pelvis exaggerates the lower-back curve and shortens apparent stature, and that stretching hip flexors while strengthening glutes and core restores it.

The exercises discussed are ordinary mobility and strength work; sources report no specific harms. Persistent tilt asymmetry can relate to scoliosis or leg-length differences, which Wikipedia says are addressed by clinicians.

lead: Posture for height is the belief in looksmaxxing communities that correcting pelvic tilt, rib flare or related posture patterns can add centimetres to standing height. Forum threads on anterior pelvic tilt (APT) ask whether fixing it would increase height, how to correct it, and whether tilt asymmetry affects facial symmetry.[1][2][3]

Pelvic tilt is the orientation of the pelvis relative to the thigh bones and trunk, and Wikipedia describes anterior, posterior and lateral forms with associated muscle patterns and exercise suggestions, noting the article's height link appears only in an image caption and that no effectiveness data are given.[4] Clinical literature on pelvic tilt concerns spinopelvic alignment and its relation to pain and disability in spinal deformity,[5][6] not height gain in healthy people.
infobox: Anterior pelvic tilt, posterior tilt, lateral tilt, rib flare
Hip flexor stretching, glute and core strengthening[4][14]

paras: Wikipedia defines anterior pelvic tilt as the front of the pelvis dropping relative to the back, attributed to shortened hip flexors and lengthened hip extensors, and associated with an exaggerated lower-back curve.[4] Posterior tilt is the opposite pattern, and lateral tilt is linked to scoliosis or unequal leg length.[4] Clinical papers describe pelvic incidence as a fixed anatomical parameter, while pelvic tilt and sacral slope are positional and adjust to compensate for spinal curvature.[7][8]

Proponents hold that an exaggerated lower-back curve and tilted pelvis shorten apparent stature and that correcting it recovers lost inches. In one looksmax.org post, a user reports growing from 5'11 to 6'1 after addressing APT through hip flexor stretching, hip thrusts and abdominal and glute training, and a separate poster with scoliosis and APT estimates he could be one to two inches taller without them.[3][2] Other threads are titled around whether correction raises height or adds 2 cm quickly.[9][10]

A 2024 systematic review with meta-analysis assessed whether stretching or strengthening exercise changes spinal and lumbopelvic posture, including pelvic tilt and lordosis, in healthy people, and rated the certainty of evidence using GRADE.[11] Radiographic studies of asymptomatic people and of adult spinal deformity establish normal ranges and link sagittal misalignment to pain and disability.[5][6][12]
Wikipedia notes that its pelvic tilt exercise section carries source-reliability tags and reports no effectiveness data.[4] No study located measured whole-body stature change after tilt correction.

The topic is discussed in height and body-symmetry threads. One poster asks whether pelvic tilt causes facial asymmetry and another replies that body symmetry affects face symmetry, while a further reply says it cannot be changed while one has it.[1] A user with APT reports that stretches had no effect for him.[2]

No studies found on pelvic tilt or rib posture correction for increasing stature in healthy people. Related research includes the 2024 meta-analysis of stretching and strengthening for posture,[11] and a registered trial of standing trunk extension and spinal height in people with low back pain (NCT03785457).[13]

lore.intro: Posture threads on looksmax.org frame pelvic tilt as lost height or as a driver of asymmetry, and mostly report personal accounts.[1][2][3]
